protocolBuilder.narrativePedigree.atRisk: Optionally show possible (at-risk) statuses alongside the certain ones, inferred from family structure and inheritance patterns.

Two rules constrain how risk travels through a family. Only biological and donor relationships pass conditions on; social, adoptive, surrogate and partner links do not. And where a person’s biological sex is not known, sex-linked inheritance through that person is left uncertain rather than guessed.

At-risk statuses are not observed or diagnosed. They are inferred from the family structure together with each condition’s inheritance pattern — the child of a parent affected by a dominant condition and the child of two carriers of a recessive condition are both shown as may develop it, while a child with only one carrier parent is shown as may carry it.

When this is on, the pedigree also shows a person who may develop a condition or may carry it. These are drawn as the usual status symbol with a question mark (“?”) added. A solid, filled symbol always means a clinically affected individual (per Bennett et al., 2022 nomenclature), so at-risk relatives always appear as unfilled symbols marked with a “?”.

At-risk symbols are a strong visual signal that can be read as established fact rather than inferred risk. They are intended for clinician-directed use, where the result is interpreted in context. Standard pedigree nomenclature (Bennett et al., 2022) deliberately does not encode probabilistic risk, so leave this off unless a clinician is guiding interpretation.
